title: EU data-path policy: allowlist/denylist precedence and fallback routing
creator: Priya Patel
description: Goal: Implement a deterministic EU data-path routing policy that enforces customer-specific residency constraints while supporting tier routing and safe fallback model variants. This ticket covers policy semantics, enforcement modes (hard vs soft), audit logging, metrics, and a safe rollout path.
details: Background: Several enterprise customers require strict EU-only residency or routing allowlists/denylists. We must ensure requests from these tenants never leave EU regions unless explicitly allowed. Secondary goals: preserve low-latency tier routing (e.g., premium vs standard) and provide graceful fallback model variants when exact model+region combos are unavailable. The implementation must be observable and reversible for canarying.
policy_spec_excerpt:
Policy evaluation order (highest -> lowest precedence):
  1) Explicit denylist entry for customer or account ID -> immediate block (hard enforcement) or annotated denial in soft mode.
  2) Customer allowlist of regions/tier -> attempt to route to matching region + tier.
  3) Global residency constraints (eg. EU-only tag at account level) -> restrict candidate region set to EU regions only.
  4) Fallback rules: bandwidth/capacity fallback, and model-variant fallback (see fallback rules).
Important: denylist entries MUST override any allowlist or fallback. This is a security-first decision after legal review.
fallback_rules:
When a requested region+tier+model is not available: 
  - First: try compatible local model variant (e.g., smaller quantized variant verified for same output contract) in same region.
  - Second: try same model family on a different EU region (respecting residency).
  - Third: if policy allows cross-region egress (explicit per-customer opt-in), route to permitted external region.
  - Final: if none allowed and policy is hard-enforced -> return 409/451 with policy reason. If soft mode -> return best-effort path and emit telemetry indicating policy violation.
We add a circuit-breaker to prevent bulk cross-region failovers: if >X% of EU requests are routed cross-region due to capacity within Y minutes, throttle fallbacks and surface PagerDuty alert.
observability_and_metrics: Must emit: policy.decisions.(allow|deny|fallback), policy.reason codes, candidate_region_list length, fallbacks.invoked, fallback.type (variant|region|egress), and per-customer policy_violation_count. Dashboards: EU Routing compliance by customer, 95/99th latency for routed vs fallback, and cross-region egress rate. Create dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/abc123/eu-routing-compliance
audit_and_logging: Every decision must be logged to the audit pipeline with: timestamp, customer_id, request_id, matched_policy_version, decision, candidates_considered, final_route, and user-visible error code when blocked. Audit logs stored for 1 year for enterprise customers (configurable per account).
rollout_plan:
1) Feature flag + soft enforcement (telemetry-only) for 2 weeks in staging.
2) Canary: enable hard enforcement for 3 low-risk customers in EU (week 1).
3) Expand canary to 20 customers + add automated circuit-breaker thresholds (week 2).
4) Full launch to all EU-bound accounts after security/legal sign-off and metrics OK (week 3).
5) Post-launch: monitor SLOs and run a 30-day regression evaluation on quality metrics for model-variant fallbacks.
tradeoffs_and_decisions:
- Precedence: choose denylist > allowlist to minimize legal exposure (Decision made 2026-02-25 after Legal consult).
- Soft vs hard enforcement: start in soft mode to catch misconfigurations; many customers asked for hard-by-default but we agreed to staged approach.
- Fallback quality vs availability: fallback to quantized variants may slightly degrade output; add per-customer opt-in for quality-sensitive workloads.
